what_its_for: Metyrapone is used to test how well your adrenal glands and pituitary gland are working together. It is also sometimes used to treat a condition called Cushing's syndrome, where your body makes too much of a stress hormone called cortisol. Your doctor may use this medicine to help bring your cortisol levels down to a safer range.
how_to_take: Take metyrapone by mouth with food or milk to help prevent stomach upset. Swallow the capsules whole with a full glass of water. Take it exactly as your doctor tells you — do not take more or less than prescribed. If you are taking it for a diagnostic test, follow your doctor's specific instructions very carefully about when and how much to take, as timing is very important for accurate test results.
dosing: For a diagnostic test: Your doctor will usually give you a single dose (typically 30 mg per kilogram of your body weight, or about 2 grams for most adults) taken at midnight the night before your blood test the next morning. For treating Cushing's syndrome: Doses are usually between 500 mg and 6,000 mg per day, divided into several doses taken throughout the day. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on your hormone levels and how you respond to the medicine. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and are taking this medicine regularly for Cushing's syndrome, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you miss your dose during a diagnostic test, call your doctor right away, as the test may need to be rescheduled.
storage: Store metyrapone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking metyrapone, as it can make side effects like dizziness worse. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because many drugs can interact with metyrapone — including phenytoin (Dilantin), rifampin, acetaminophen (Tylenol), and some hormone medicines. Avoid making changes to your diet or other medications without checking with your doctor first, as this can affect your cortisol levels.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe dizziness or fainting, extreme tiredness or weakness, severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain, signs of low cortisol (adrenal crisis) such as severe weakness, confusion, fast heartbeat, or feeling like you might pass out, unusual weight gain or swelling, skin rash or allergic reaction (hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat), or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before continuing this medicine.
when_it_works: For a diagnostic test, metyrapone works within a few hours of taking it, and your doctor will check your blood or urine the next morning to see how your body responded. For treating Cushing's syndrome, you may start to notice some improvement in symptoms within a few days to a couple of weeks, but it may take several weeks to see the full benefit. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to monitor your hormone levels and adjust your dose as needed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine should generally not be used during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary, as it can harm the unborn baby and may cause adrenal problems. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if metyrapone passes into breast milk, so talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Metyrapone can be used in children for diagnostic testing, but dosing must be carefully calculated by your doctor based on your child's weight. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness, so extra caution and close monitoring are needed. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how your body processes this medicine.
